text: Dame Gillian Phyllida Barlow DBE RA (4 April 1944 – 12 March 2023) was a British visual artist who studied at Chelsea College of Art from 1960 to 1963 and the Slade School of Art from 1963 to 1966. She joined the Slade faculty in the late 1960s and taught there for over forty years, retiring in 2009 as an emerita professor of fine art. Her students included Rachel Whiteread and Ángela de la Cruz, and she significantly influenced younger artists. Born in Newcastle upon Tyne in 1944, the daughter of psychiatrist Erasmus Darwin Barlow, a great-grandson of Charles Darwin, she was raised in London after the Second World War, where her experiences of bomb damage deeply informed her artistic practice. At Chelsea, she studied under George Fullard, whose teachings emphasized the adventure of making, and she developed a fascination with the potential of materials like cardboard, polystyrene, scrim, and cement. She found a strong affinity for clay and focused on creating abstract works that invited viewers to engage with the materials and processes. Barlow believed art schools overemphasized a single model of artistic success. After graduating from the Slade in 1966, she began teaching at the West of England College of Art (now the University of the West of England, Bristol), where she learned traditional sculpture techniques and discovered the malleability of clay. In 2004, she was appointed professor of fine art and director of undergraduate studies at the Slade before retiring in 2009. Her artistic breakthrough came in 2004 when her work was shown at the BALTIC, Gateshead, followed by representation by Hauser & Wirth. In 2018 and 2019, she served as 'provocateur' for the Yorkshire Sculpture international. Barlow’s work combines playful, childlike colours with industrial materials and large scale, creating forms that appear both heavy and light, imposing and unstable. Her sculptures often evoke a sense of environment, blocking or interrupting space, and she openly exposed her processes and materials. Known for her use of inexpensive materials such as plywood, cardboard, plaster, cement, fabric, and paint, her practice is rooted in an anti-monumental tradition, drawing on everyday objects and physical material handling. Her works have been exhibited globally, including a solo show at the Duveen Galleries at Tate Britain in 2014, a solo exhibition titled HOARD at The Norton Museum of Art in 2013 as part of the RAW – Recognition of Art by Women – series, and a show called 'Set' at the Fruitmarket Gallery in Edinburgh in 2015. In 2016, she exhibited at the Kunsthalle Zurich and was one of four artists nominated for the inaugural Hepworth Prize, with her work displayed at Hepworth Wakefield. For the 2017 Venice Biennale, she presented her Folly series, which occupied both indoor and outdoor spaces; initially planned as hanging 'baubles' from the pavilion facade, the installation was altered due to cost and instead resembled lollipops. She was selected for her "challenging and imposing sculptures" and commanded a powerful presence at the 57th Biennale. In 2018, she had solo exhibitions at Hauser & Wirth in New York titled 'tilt', with High Line Art in New York titled 'prop', and at Jupiter Artland in Edinburgh titled 'Quarry'. In 2019, the Royal Academy of Art hosted a site-specific exhibition of her large-scale, brutalist sculptures titled cultural-de-sac in the Gabrielle Jungels-Winkler Galleries, responding to the RA’s architecture. Barlow was elected a Royal Academician in 2011, awarded a CBE in the 2015 New Year Honours for services to the arts, and promoted to DBE in the 2021 Birthday Honours for services to art. She was also a member of the juries that selected Doris Salcedo (2016), Pierre Huyghe (2017), Isa Genzken (2019), and Michael Rakowitz (2020) for the Nasher Prize. Barlow died on 12 March 2023, at the age of 78.
